claim: Perceived cues signaling others' pain induce empathy which in turn motivates altruistic behavior toward those who appear suffering.
source: Perceived cues signaling others' pain induce empathy which in turn motivates altruistic behavior toward those who appear suffering.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that is supported by the entire body of experimental work presented in the manuscript.

claim: Lack of BOP reduces subjective estimation of others' painful feelings.
source: We show evidence that lack of BOP reduces subjective estimation of others' painful feelings and decreases monetary donations to those who show pain expressions.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from Experiments 1 and 2 showing reduced pain intensity ratings when BOP was decreased.

claim: Lack of BOP decreases monetary donations to those who show pain expressions.
source: We show evidence that lack of BOP reduces subjective estimation of others' painful feelings and decreases monetary donations to those who show pain expressions.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from Experiments 1 and 2 showing reduced monetary donations when BOP was decreased.

claim: Lack of BOP attenuates neural responses to pain expressions within 200 ms after face onset.
source: Moreover, lack of BOP attenuates neural responses to their pain expressions within 200 ms after face onset and modulates neural responses to others' pain in the insular, post-central, and frontal cortices.
evidence: This claim is supported by EEG data from Experiments 3 and 5 showing reduced P2 amplitudes to pain expressions of actors/actresses compared to patients.

claim: Lack of BOP modulates neural responses to others' pain in the insular, post-central, and frontal cortices.
source: Moreover, lack of BOP attenuates neural responses to their pain expressions within 200 ms after face onset and modulates neural responses to others' pain in the insular, post-central, and frontal cortices.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data from Experiment 6 showing modulations in these brain regions.

claim: BOP provide a cognitive basis of human empathy and altruism.
source: Our findings suggest that BOP provide a cognitive basis of human empathy and altruism and unravel the intermediate neural mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined behavioral and neuroimaging findings across all experiments.

claim: Empathy refers to understanding and sharing of others' emotional states.
source: Empathy refers to understanding and sharing of others' emotional states (Decety and Jackson, 2004) and has been proposed to provide a key motivation for altruistic behavior in both humans and animals (Batson et al., 2015; de Waal, 2008; Decety et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Empathy has been proposed to provide a key motivation for altruistic behavior in both humans and animals.
source: Empathy refers to understanding and sharing of others' emotional states (Decety and Jackson, 2004) and has been proposed to provide a key motivation for altruistic behavior in both humans and animals (Batson et al., 2015; de Waal, 2008; Decety et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Empathy can be induced by perceived cues signaling others' pain that activate neural responses in brain regions underlying sensorimotor resonance, affective sharing, and mental state inference/perspective-taking.
source: Empathy can be induced by perceived cues signaling others' pain that activate neural responses in brain regions underlying sensorimotor resonance (e.g., the sensorimotor cortex), affective sharing (e.g., the anterior insula [AI] and anterior cingulate cortex [ACC]), and mental state inference/perspective-taking (e.g., the medial prefrontal cortex [mPFC] and temporoparietal junction [TPJ]) (Singer et al., 2004; Jackson et al., 2005; Avenanti et al., 2005; Saarela et al., 2007; Fan and Han, 2008; Shamay-Tsoory et al., 2009; Han et al., 2009; Sheng and Han, 2012; Fan et al., 2011; Lamm et al., 2011; Zhou and Han, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to previous neuroimaging research.

claim: Neural responses to others' pain in the empathy network and functional connectivity between its key hubs can predict motives for subsequent altruistic actions.
source: Neural responses to others' pain in the empathy network and functional connectivity between its key hubs can predict motives for subsequent altruistic actions (e.g., Hein et al., 2010; Hein et al., 2016; Mathur et al., 2010; Luo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Empathic neural responses are influenced by multiple factors such as perceptual features depicting others' pain, observers' perspectives and attention, and perceived social relationships between observers and empathy targets.
source: However, empathic neural responses are influenced by multiple factors such as perceptual features depicting others' pain (Gu and Han, 2007; Li and Han, 2019), observers' perspectives and attention (Gu and Han, 2007; Li and Han, 2010; Jauniaux et al., 2019), and perceived social relationships between observers and empathy targets (Xu et al., 2009; Avenanti et al., 2010; Hein et al., 2010; Mathur et al., 2010; Sheng and Han, 2012; Azevedo et al., 2013; Sheng et al., 2014; Sheng et al., 2016; Han, 2018; Zhou and Han, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Beliefs refer to mental representations of something that are not immediately present to the scenes but allow people to think beyond what is here and now.
source: Beliefs refer to mental representations of something that are not immediately present to the scenes but allow people to think beyond what is here and now (Fuentes, 2019).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation.

claim: Beliefs reflect an organism's endorsement of a particular state of affairs as actual.
source: Beliefs reflect an organism's endorsement of a particular state of affairs as actual (McKay and Dennett, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: Beliefs that best approximate reality enable the believers to act effectively and maximize their survival.
source: Beliefs that best approximate reality enable the believers to act effectively and maximize their survival (Fodor, 1985; Millikan, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Beliefs affect multiple mental processes such as visual awareness and processing of emotions including experiences of pain.
source: Previous research has shown that beliefs affect multiple mental processes such as visual awareness (Sterzer et al., 2008) and processing of emotions (Petrovic et al., 2005) including experiences of pain (Wager et al., 2004; Colloca and Benedetti, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The function of beliefs is manifested in increasing the efficiency of neural processes involved in decision-making and goal setting.
source: The function of beliefs is also manifested in increasing the efficiency of neural processes involved in decision-making and goal setting (Garcés and Finkel, 2019; Régner et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Functional magnetic resonance imaging of brain activity suggested modulations of insular responses to perceived pain by beliefs of anesthetization.
source: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) of brain activity suggested modulations of insular responses to perceived pain by beliefs of anesthetization.
evidence: This claim refers to findings from Lamm et al., 2007 study mentioned in the text.

claim: Patient-identity change significantly reduced perceived pain intensity in the 2nd_round (vs. 1st_round) test.
source: Specifically, patient-identity change (i.e., from patients to actors/actresses) significantly reduced perceived pain intensity and amounts of monetary donations in the 2nd_round (vs. 1st_round) test (F(1,59)=82.664 and 34.542, ps<0.001, ηp2=0.584 and 0.369, 90% CI=[0.440, 0.673] and [0.207, 0.495]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 1.

claim: Patient-identity change significantly reduced amounts of monetary donations in the 2nd_round (vs. 1st_round) test.
source: Specifically, patient-identity change (i.e., from patients to actors/actresses) significantly reduced perceived pain intensity and amounts of monetary donations in the 2nd_round (vs. 1st_round) test (F(1,59)=82.664 and 34.542, ps<0.001, ηp2=0.584 and 0.369, 90% CI=[0.440, 0.673] and [0.207, 0.495]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 1.

claim: Patient-identity repetition significantly increased both perceived pain intensity and monetary donations in the 2nd_round (vs. 1st_round) test.
source: By contrast, patient-identity repetition significantly increased both perceived pain intensity and monetary donations in the 2nd_round (vs. 1st_round) test (F(1,59)=36.060 and 27.457, ps<0.001, ηp2=0.379 and 0.318, 90% CI=[0.216, 0.503] and [0.159, 0.449]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 1.

claim: The rating scores of pain intensity of faces whose identities changed from patient to actor/actress significantly predicted the amount of monetary donations in the 1st_round test but not in the 2nd_round test.
source: The results showed that the rating scores of pain intensity of faces whose identities changed from patient in the 1st_round test to actor/actress in the 2nd_round test significantly predicted the amount of monetary donations in the 1st_round test but not in the 2nd_round test (r=0.608 and 0.187, p<0.001 and p=0.152, 95% CI=[0.422, 0.776] and [−0.069, 0.435], all results were false discovery rate-corrected, Figure 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 1 and illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: Rating scores of pain intensity partially mediated the relationship between patient-identity change and reduced amount of monetary donations.
source: The first mediation analysis showed that rating scores of pain intensity partially mediated the relationship between patient-identity change and reduced amount of monetary donations (direct effect: c′=−0.902, t(118)=−2.468, p=0.015, 95% CI=[−1.626, –0.178]; indirect effect: a×b=−0.839, 95% CI=[−1.455, –0.374], Figure 1e, see Supplementary file 1 for statistical details).
evidence: This claim is supported by mediation analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 1 and illustrated in Figure 1e.

claim: Rating scores of pain intensity mediated the relationship between patient-identity repetition and increased amount of monetary donations.
source: The second mediation analysis showed evidence that the rating scores of pain intensity also mediated the relationship between patient-identity repetition and increased amount of monetary donations (direct effect: c′=0.028, t(118)=0.072, p=0.943, 95% CI=[−0.727, 0.782]; indirect effect: a×b=0.885, 95% CI=[0.314, 1.563], Figure 1f, see Supplementary file 2 for statistical details).
evidence: This claim is supported by mediation analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 1 and illustrated in Figure 1f.

claim: A larger score of treatment effectiveness (i.e., a weaker intrinsic BOP related to a face) predicted weaker empathy and less monetary donations related to that face.
source: One-sample t-tests revealed that the z-values were significantly smaller than 0 (correlations between intrinsic BOP and pain intensity/unpleasantness/monetary donation: mean±s.d.=−0.631±0.531, –0.643±0.524, and −0.469±0.529; t(59)=−9.213, –9.501, and −6.875; ps<0.001; Cohen's d=1.188, 1.227, and 0.887; 95% CI=[−0.768, –0.494], [−0.778, –0.507], and [−0.606, –0.333], Figure 2a–c), suggesting that a larger score of treatment effectiveness (i.e., a weaker intrinsic BOP related to a face) predicted weaker empathy and less monetary donations relate to that face.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 2 and illustrated in Figure 2a-c.

claim: Decreasing internal BOP resulted in lower subjective evaluation of others' pain and one's own unpleasantness and less monetary donations in the 2nd_round vs. 1st_round test.
source: The results showed that decreasing internal BOP (i.e., for 100% effective target faces) resulted in lower subjective evaluation of others' pain and one's own unpleasantness and less monetary donations in the 2nd_round vs. 1st_round test, whereas enhancing BOP (i.e., for 0% effective target faces) produced opposite effects (Figure 2d–f, see Supplementary file 3 for statistical details).
evidence: This claim is supported by ANOVA analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 2 and illustrated in Figure 2d-f.

claim: Enhancing BOP produced opposite effects to decreasing BOP on subjective evaluation of others' pain and one's own unpleasantness and monetary donations.
source: The results showed that decreasing internal BOP (i.e., for 100% effective target faces) resulted in lower subjective evaluation of others' pain and one's own unpleasantness and less monetary donations in the 2nd_round vs. 1st_round test, whereas enhancing BOP (i.e., for 0% effective target faces) produced opposite effects (Figure 2d–f, see Supplementary file 3 for statistical details).
evidence: This claim is supported by ANOVA analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 2 and illustrated in Figure 2d-f.

claim: Rating scores of pain intensity partially mediated the relationship between decreased BOP and monetary donations.
source: Furthermore, the results of mediation analyses showed that rating scores of pain intensity partially mediated the relationship between decreased BOP (i.e., for '100% effective' patients) and monetary donations (direct effect: c′=−0.038, t(58)=−3.657, p<0.001, 95% CI=[−0.059, 0.017]; indirect effect: a×b=−0.016, 95% CI=[−0.027, –0.005], Figure 2k, see Supplementary file 4 for statistical details).
evidence: This claim is supported by mediation analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 2 and illustrated in Figure 2k.

claim: Rating scores of unpleasantness did not mediate the relationship between decreased BOP and monetary donations.
source: However, rating scores of unpleasantness did not mediate the relationship between decreased BOP and monetary donations (indirect effect: a×b=−0.002, 95% CI=[−0.009, 0.003]).
evidence: This claim is supported by mediation analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 2.

claim: Neither pain intensity nor unpleasantness ratings mediated the relationship between enhanced BOP and monetary donations.
source: Neither pain intensity nor unpleasantness ratings mediated the relationship between enhanced BOP (i.e., for '0% effective' patients) and monetary donations (indirect effect: a×b=0.003 and −0.002, 95% CI=[−0.009, 0.013] and [−0.007, 0.004], Figure 2l, see Supplementary files 5, 6, and 7 for statistical details).
evidence: This claim is supported by mediation analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 2 and illustrated in Figure 2l.

claim: Decreased BOP influences altruistic decisions possibly via modulations of the cognitive component of empathy rather than the affective component of empathy.
source: These behavioral results suggest that decreased BOP influences altruistic decisions possibly via modulations of the cognitive component of empathy (i.e., understanding others' pain) rather than the affective component of empathy (i.e., sharing others' pain).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mediation analysis results showing that pain intensity but not unpleasantness mediated the BOP-donation relationship.

claim: A larger score of belief of patient identities significantly predicted greater subjective feelings of pain intensity related to patients' pain (vs. neutral) expressions.
source: Moreover, a larger score of belief of patient identities significantly predicted greater subjective feelings of pain intensity related to patients' pain (vs. neutral) expressions (r=0.384, p=0.036, 95% CI=[0.074, 0.627]), whereas there was no significant association between belief scores and subjective feelings of pain intensity related to actors/actresses' pain (vs. neutral) expressions (r=0.264, p=0.159, 95% CI=[−0.162, 0.605]).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 3.

claim: The P2 amplitude was significantly greater to pain versus neutral expressions of patients' faces.
source: Simple effect analyses verified significantly greater P2 amplitudes to pain versus neutral expressions of patients' faces (F(1,29)=18.059, p<0.001, ηp2=0.384, 90% CI=[0.150, 0.546]), whereas the P2 amplitude did not differ significantly between pain and neutral expressions of actors/actresses' faces (F(1,29)=0.334, p=0.568, ηp2=0.011, 90% CI=[0.000, 0.135], Figure 3b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by ERP analysis from Experiment 3 and illustrated in Figure 3b and c.

claim: The P2 amplitude did not differ significantly between pain and neutral expressions of actors/actresses' faces.
source: Simple effect analyses verified significantly greater P2 amplitudes to pain versus neutral expressions of patients' faces (F(1,29)=18.059, p<0.001, ηp2=0.384, 90% CI=[0.150, 0.546]), whereas the P2 amplitude did not differ significantly between pain and neutral expressions of actors/actresses' faces (F(1,29)=0.334, p=0.568, ηp2=0.011, 90% CI=[0.000, 0.135], Figure 3b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by ERP analysis from Experiment 3 and illustrated in Figure 3b and c.

claim: Lack of BOP significantly weakens early empathic neural responses to others' pain within 200 ms after stimulus onset.
source: This finding indicates that lack of BOP significantly weakens early empathic neural responses to others' pain within 200 ms after stimulus onset.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ERP results in Experiment 3 showing reduced P2 amplitudes to actors/actresses' pain expressions.

claim: Rating scores of pain intensity did not differ significantly between faces from the two teams in Experiment 4.
source: Rating scores of pain intensity did not differ significantly between faces from the two teams (F(1,29)=1.608, p=0.215, ηp2=0.053, 90% CI=[0, 0.216], Bayes factors=0.261, Figure 4a, see Supplementary file 10 for details).
evidence: This claim is supported by ANOVA analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 4 and illustrated in Figure 4a.

claim: The P2 amplitude was enlarged by pain compared to neutral expressions in Experiment 4.
source: ANOVAs of the mean P2 amplitudes over the frontal electrodes revealed a significant main effect of facial expression (F(1,29)=12.182, p=0.002, ηp2=0.296, 90% CI=[0.081, 0.473], Figure 4b and c, see Supplementary file 11 for details), as the P2 amplitude was enlarged by pain compared to neutral expressions.
evidence: This claim is supported by ERP analysis from Experiment 4 and illustrated in Figure 4b and c.

claim: The effect of pain expression on P2 amplitude did not differ significantly between faces from the two teams in Experiment 4.
source: However, this effect did not differ significantly between faces from the two teams (F(1,29)=0.040, p=0.843, ηp2=0.001, 90% CI=[0, 0.053], Bayes factors=0.258).
evidence: This claim is supported by ERP analysis from Experiment 4.

claim: BOP, but not other cognitive processes involved in the experimental manipulations, plays a key role in modulations of neural responses to others' pain.
source: Taken together, the results in Experiments 3 and 4 suggest a key role of BOP, but not other cognitive processes involved in the experimental manipulations, in modulations of neural responses to others' pain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the results of Experiments 3 and 4.

claim: The D score from the implicit association test was significantly larger than 0 in Experiment 5.
source: One-sample t-test revealed that the D score was significantly larger than 0 (0.929±0.418, t(29)=12.178, p<0.001, Cohen's d=2.223, 95% CI=[0.773, 1.085]), suggesting that patient faces were more strongly associated with patient relevant words whereas actor/actress faces were more strongly associated with actor/actress relevant words.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of IAT data from Experiment 5.

claim: Patient faces were more strongly associated with patient relevant words whereas actor/actress faces were more strongly associated with actor/actress relevant words in Experiment 5.
source: One-sample t-test revealed that the D score was significantly larger than 0 (0.929±0.418, t(29)=12.178, p<0.001, Cohen's d=2.223, 95% CI=[0.773, 1.085]), suggesting that patient faces were more strongly associated with patient relevant words whereas actor/actress faces were more strongly associated with actor/actress relevant words.
evidence: This is an inference from the IAT results in Experiment 5.

claim: Decreasing BOP significantly reduced self-report of others' pain and monetary donations in Experiment 5.
source: In particular, decreasing BOP (i.e., changing patient identity in the 1st_round test to actor/actress identity in the 2nd_round test) significantly reduced self-report of others' pain and monetary donations (Test Phase×Identity Change) interactions on rating scores of pain intensity and amounts of monetary donations: (F(1,29)=59.654 and 129.696, ps<0.001, ηp2=0.673 and 0.817, 90% CI=[0.479, 0.764] and [0.694, 0.868]); effects of patient-to-actor/actress identity change on rating scores of pain intensity and amounts of monetary donations: (F(1,29)=58.196 and 180.022, ps<0.001, ηp2=0.667 and 0.861, 90% CI=[0.472, 0.760] and [0.765, 0.900], Figure 5a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by ANOVA analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 5 and illustrated in Figure 5a and b.

claim: Lack of BOP significantly decreased P2 amplitudes to pain (vs. neutral) expressions of actor/actress compared to patient faces in Experiment 5.
source: The EEG results replicated those in Experiment 3 by showing significantly deceased P2 amplitudes to pain (vs. neutral) expressions of actor/actress compared to patient faces (Identity×Expression interaction: F(1,29)=9.494, p=0.004, ηp2=0.247, 90% CI=[0.050, 0.429], Figure 5c and d, see Supplementary file 12 for statistical details).
evidence: This claim is supported by ERP analysis from Experiment 5 and illustrated in Figure 5c and d.

claim: Subjective feelings of others' pain mediated the association between patient-identity change and reduced monetary donations.
source: The effect sizes of the indirect path (2) and (3) were 25.26% and 5.58%, respectively, indicating that subjective feelings of others' pain mediated the association between patient-identity change and reduced monetary donations.
evidence: This claim is supported by serial mediation analysis of behavioral and EEG data from Experiment 5.

claim: The mediator role of subjective feelings of others' pain was partially mediated by BOP-induced variations of empathic brain activity in response to others' pain expressions.
source: Moreover, this mediator role was partially mediated by BOP-induced variations of empathic brain activity in response to others' pain expressions.
evidence: This claim is supported by serial mediation analysis of behavioral and EEG data from Experiment 5.

claim: Viewing video clips or pictures showing faces with pain versus neutral expressions induced activations in the ACC, AI, and inferior parietal cortex.
source: fMRI studies found that viewing video clips (Botvinick et al., 2005) or pictures (Sheng et al., 2014) showing faces with pain versus neutral expressions or viewing photos of faces of patients who were suffering from provoked pain versus chronic pain (Saarela et al., 2007) induced activations in the ACC, AI, and inferior parietal cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous fMRI research.

claim: The cortical areas activated by facial expressions of pain were also engaged by the first-hand experience of pain evoked by thermal stimulation.
source: Moreover, the cortical areas activated by facial expressions of pain were also engaged by the first-hand experience of pain evoked by thermal stimulation (Botvinick et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The strengths of AI activations during observation of others' pain were correlated with subjective feelings of others' pain.
source: Moreover, the strengths of AI activations during observation of others' pain were correlated with subjective feelings of others' pain (Saarela et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Neural responses to pain expressions occurred as early as 130 ms after face onset over the frontal/central regions as indexed by the increased amplitude of a positive component at 128–188 ms (P2) in response to pain compared neutral expressions.
source: ERP studies found that neural responses to pain expressions occurred as early as 130 ms after face onset over the frontal/central regions as indexed by the increased amplitude of a positive component at 128–188 ms (P2) in response to pain compared neutral expressions (Sheng and Han, 2012; Sheng et al., 2013; Sheng et al., 2016; Han et al., 2016; Li and Han, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous ERP research.

claim: The P2 amplitudes in response to others' pain expressions positively predicted subjective feelings of own unpleasantness induced by others' pain and self-reports of one's own empathy traits.
source: In addition, the P2 amplitudes in response to others' pain expressions positively predicted subjective feelings of own unpleasantness induced by others' pain and self-reports of one's own empathy traits (Sheng and Han, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Source estimation of the P2 component in response to others' pain expressions suggested a possible origin in the ACC.
source: In addition, source estimation of the P2 component in response to others' pain expressions suggested a possible origin in the ACC.
evidence: This claim is based on previous research findings mentioned in the text.

claim: Perceived painful versus non-painful stimuli applied to targets activated the bilateral AI/inferior frontal cortex, bilateral inferior and superior temporal gyri, mPFC, left inferior parietal lobe, right superior parietal lobe, and right post-central gyrus and posterior insula.
source: This analysis revealed significant activations in the cognitive, affective, and sensorimotor nodes of the empathy network, including the bilateral AI/inferior frontal cortex (Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) peak coordinates x/y/z=−45/17/–5 and 45/26/–8), bilateral inferior and superior temporal gyri (−48/–70/−2 and 51/–58/−5), mPFC (3/56/25), left inferior parietal lobe (−63/−25/31), right superior parietal lobe (30/−58/55), and right post-central gyrus and posterior insula (58/−25/26, Figure 6a; all activations were identified using a combined threshold of voxel-level p< 0.001, uncorrected, and cluster-level p<0.05, Family-wise error (FWE)-corrected).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI analysis from Experiment 6 and illustrated in Figure 6a.

claim: Non-painful stimulations to patient versus actor/actress activated the mPFC and bilateral TPJ.
source: This analysis showed significant activations in the mPFC (−6/59/25) and bilateral TPJ (−54/−58/28 and 57/−67/31, Figure 6b; all activations were identified using a combined threshold of voxel-level p<0.001, uncorrected, and cluster-level p<0.05, FWE-corrected).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI analysis from Experiment 6 and illustrated in Figure 6b.

claim: The searchlight RSA revealed significant activations in the left AI and inferior parietal cortex, and the right AI/frontal cortex, superior temporal gyrus, inferior post-central gyrus, and superior parietal cortex.
source: The results revealed significant activations in the left AI (MNI peak coordinates x/y/z=−39/20/8) and inferior parietal cortex (−60/−19/29), and the right AI/frontal cortex (36/23/11), superior temporal gyrus (54/−37/11), inferior post-central gyrus (63/−40/26), and superior parietal cortex (39/−49/50) (Figure 6d).
evidence: This claim is supported by RSA analysis of fMRI data from Experiment 6 and illustrated in Figure 6d.

claim: Activities in the VPS pattern were significantly decreased in response to video clips showing actors/actresses' compared to patients' pain.
source: The results showed that activities in the VPS pattern were significantly decreased in response to video clips showing actors/actresses' compared to patients' pain (Figure 6e and f, body-specific VPS: mean±s.d.=41.487±28.794 vs. 46.548±32.051, t(30)=−2.059, p(one-tailed)=0.024, BF+0=2.361; general VPS: mean±s.d.=1.188±6.058 vs. 2.462±6.997, t(30)=−2.447, p(one-tailed)=0.010, BF+0=4.820).
evidence: This claim is supported by VPS analysis of fMRI data from Experiment 6 and illustrated in Figure 6e and f.

claim: Activities in the brain regions supporting affective sharing, empathic sensorimotor resonance, and emotion regulation may provide intermediate mechanisms underlying variations of subjective feelings of others' pain intensity due to lack of BOP.
source: These fMRI results together suggest that activities in the brain regions supporting affective sharing (e.g., insula; Shamay-Tsoory et al., 2009; Fan et al., 2011; Lamm et al., 2019), empathic sensorimotor resonance (e.g., post-central gyrus; Avenanti et al., 2005; Zhou and Han, 2021), and emotion regulation (e.g., lateral frontal cortex; Ochsner and Gross, 2005; Etkin et al., 2015) may provide intermediate mechanisms underlying variations of subjective feelings of others' pain intensity due to lack of BOP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fMRI results in Experiment 6, supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Perceived information about social relationships between observers and empathy targets modulates empathic neural responses.
source: Perceived information about social relationships between observers and empathy targets also modulates empathic neural responses such that, relative to viewing own-race or own-team individuals' pain, viewing other-race or opponent-team individuals' pain decreased empathic neural responses in the affective (e.g., ACC and AI), cognitive (e.g., mPFC and TPJ), and sensorimotor (e.g., motor cortex) nodes of the empathy network (Xu et al., 2009; Avenanti et al., 2010; Hein et al., 2010; Mathur et al., 2010; Sheng and Han, 2012; Sheng et al., 2014; Sheng et al., 2016; Han, 2018; Zhou and Han, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The perceived intergroup (racial) relationships between empathizers and empathy targets influenced altruistic behavior such as medical treatment.
source: The perceived intergroup (racial) relationships between empathizers and empathy targets also influenced altruistic behavior such as medical treatment (Drwecki et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: White individuals who more strongly endorsed false beliefs about biological differences between Blacks and Whites reported lower pain ratings for a Black (vs. White) target and suggested less accurate treatment recommendations.
source: There have been behavioral evidence that White individuals who more strongly endorsed false beliefs about biological differences between Blacks and Whites (e.g., 'Black people's skin is thicker than White people's skin') reported lower pain ratings for a Black (vs. White) target and suggested less accurate treatment recommendations (Hoffman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: BOP effects on empathy and altruistic behavior can be understood as modulations of empathy by preexisting internal information.
source: BOP effects on empathy and altruistic behavior can be understood as modulations of empathy by preexisting internal information (e.g., beliefs) whereas previous findings revealed modulations of empathy by instantly perceived social information in a specific social context.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current findings in the context of previous research.

claim: The BOP effects on empathy and altruistic behavior identified in this study might take place implicitly.
source: Therefore, the BOP effects on empathy and altruistic behavior identified in our study might take place implicitly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design where BOP was manipulated through identity changes rather than explicit instructions.

claim: The placebo treatment relative to a control condition significantly attenuated activations in the ACC, AI, and subcortical structures in response to painful electric shocks but increased the prefrontal activity during anticipation of painful stimulations.
source: Moreover, the placebo treatment relative to a control condition significantly attenuated activations in the ACC, AI, and subcortical structures (e.g., the thalamus) in response to painful electric shocks but increased the prefrontal activity during anticipation of painful stimulations possibly to inhibit activity in pain processing regions (Wager et al., 2004; Wager and Atlas, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The brain regions in which empathic neural responses altered due to BOP do not overlap with those in which activities are modulated by placebo analgesia.
source: The brain regions in which empathic neural responses altered due to BOP (e.g., the lateral frontal cortex) as unraveled in the current study do not overlap with those in which activities are modulated by placebo analgesia (Atlas and Wager, 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison between the current findings and previous research on placebo effects.

claim: There may be distinct neural underpinnings of BOP effects on empathic brain activity and placebo effects on brain responses to first-hand pain experiences.
source: These results suggest that there may be distinct neural underpinnings of BOP effects on empathic brain activity and placebo effects on brain responses to first-hand pain experiences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the current findings with previous research on placebo effects.

claim: Multiple neurocognitive mechanisms are involved in ingroup bias in empathy for pain such as lack of attention and early group-based categorization of outgroup faces.
source: Previous studies suggest that multiple neurocognitive mechanisms are involved in ingroup bias in empathy for pain such as lack of attention (Sheng and Han, 2012) and early group-based categorization of outgroup faces (Zhou et al., 2020b, see Han, 2018 for review).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Lack of beliefs of authenticity of others' happiness reduced the amplitudes of a long-latency positive component (i.e., P570) over the frontal region in response to happy expressions.
source: ERP results in this experiment showed that lack of beliefs of authenticity of others' happiness (e.g., actors simulating others' happy expressions vs. awardees smiling when receiving awards) reduced the amplitudes of a long-latency positive component (i.e., P570) over the frontal region in response to happy expressions.
evidence: This claim is supported by ERP data from an additional experiment described in Appendix 1.

claim: The face identities did not affect the P2 amplitudes in response to happy (vs. neutral) expressions.
source: However, the face identities did not affect the P2 amplitudes in response to happy (vs. neutral) expressions (see Appendix 1 for statistical details).
evidence: This claim is supported by ERP data from an additional experiment described in Appendix 1.

claim: BOP or happiness affect neural responses to facial expressions in different time windows after face onset.
source: However, BOP or happiness affect neural responses to facial expressions in different time windows after face onset.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the effects of beliefs on pain and happy expressions.

claim: Empathy is supposed to originate from an evolved adaptation to quickly and automatically respond to others' emotional states during parental care that is necessary for offspring survival in humans and other species.
source: Empathy is supposed to originate from an evolved adaptation to quickly and automatically respond to others' emotional states during parental care that is necessary for offspring survival in humans and other species (de Waal, 2008; Decety, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Life experiences may set up a default belief that perceived painful stimulation to others and their facial expressions reflect individuals' actual emotional states.
source: Such life experiences may set up a default belief that perceived painful stimulation to others and their facial expressions reflect individuals' actual emotional states.
evidence: This is a theoretical speculation about how beliefs develop.

claim: This default belief provides a fundamental cognitive basis of reflexive and automatic empathy and empathic brain activity that further generates autonomic and somatic responses.
source: This default belief provides a fundamental cognitive basis of reflexive and automatic empathy and empathic brain activity that further generates autonomic and somatic responses, as suggested by the perception-action model of empathy (Preston and de Waal, 2002).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citation to a model of empathy.

claim: BOP may function as cognitive gate-control to modulate neural responses to perceived pain in others.
source: BOP in such situations may function as cognitive gate-control to modulate neural responses to perceived pain in others.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the functional role of BOP based on the experimental findings.

claim: BOP provides an important cognitive basis for survival and social adaption during social interactions.
source: In this sense, BOP also provides an important cognitive basis for survival and social adaption during social interactions.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the adaptive function of BOP.
